claim: The analysis uses 14,014 responded control trials from 10 mice (259–4,095 per mouse); 2,507 control trials without a response by 5 s are excluded from every analysis.
note: N004 includes 48 no-response pulse trials mislabelled as controls; Methods must say so

claim: On responded control trials, choice accuracy increases with coherence (0.54, 0.64, 0.71 and 0.84 correct at 9, 18, 36 and 100% coherence, mean over mice).
note: v2: N028 replaces the missing psychometric number. 16% errors at 100% coherence: legend must define fast guesses vs decision errors (glossary)

claim: Median correct RT tends to decrease with coherence (mean Spearman rho −0.49 across mice), but the trend does not survive Holm correction.
note: Pre-specified T1; Holm over K1, T1, T2; frame as consistent with rodent RDK literature (for S2)

claim: Errors tend to be faster than correct responses (mean −118 ms; 9 of 10 mice), but the difference does not survive Holm correction.
note: Pre-specified T2; cells 9/18/36% with >= 10 errors; frame as consistent with rodent RDK literature (for S2)

claim: The stimulus-aligned motion-energy kernel on control trials (0.1–0.5 s) is not distinguishable from zero.
note: Pre-specified K1; null is not evidence that mice ignore fluctuations (see C006, C017)

claim: The kernel test is underpowered: within-mouse variability of the model-predicted kernel across simulated repetitions (SD 0.2–1.1% coherence) is comparable to the predicted kernel itself (0.4–0.55% coherence).
note: v2: 'as large as' -> 'comparable to' (N027 range spans N029); predicted kernel now ledgered as N029

claim: Psychophysical kernels and chronometric signatures cannot diagnose the decision strategy in these data, in line with the finding that non-integration strategies can mimic them.
note: Motivates the model comparison; do not let it carry the thesis

claim: At group level, on held-out control trials, the common model predicts choices and RTs better than the rapid-forgetting (E) and extrema-sampling (ES) models (per 1,000 trials, mice as unit; t-test Holm p 0.037 and 0.023, dz 0.94 and 1.14; Wilcoxon Holm p 0.059 and 0.055); individually it is better by > 10 in 5/10 and 6/10 mice, and no mouse favors E or ES by > 10.
note: v2: Wilcoxon and per-mouse counts in the claim itself (P1-2). Matched-component comparison (Fig 3 panel A). Robustness analyses pending NH6

claim: At group level, the common model also predicts held-out control trials better than the paper-exact integration (DDMx) and extrema-detection (ESx) models (t-test Holm p 0.037, dz 0.98 and 0.96; Wilcoxon Holm p 0.059); individually it is better by > 10 in 6/10 mice for each, and no mouse favors either by > 10.
note: v2: Fig 3 panel B labeled 'different components and input'; confounded by components and input (E and ES are the matched controls)

claim: In paired model recovery, datasets generated by rapid forgetting (E) and by the rule's extrema model (X_ext) are scored as better fit by the common model in FP_E/20 and FP_Xext/20 datasets (Δ > 10, Clopper-Pearson 95% CI) [and, under criterion G, in a fraction FPg of synthetic 10-mouse cohorts].
note: Selection-rule input; X_ext set by NH1 (ES or ESx or none), criterion by NH2; both logged before counts are read

claim: In paired model recovery, datasets generated by the common model are scored as better fit by the common model than by E and X_ext in SENS_E/20 and SENS_Xext/20 datasets (Δ > 10, Clopper-Pearson 95% CI) [and, under criterion G, in a fraction SENSg of cohorts].
